'anchor' points at the exact paragraph (tagged with data-narr in index.html) that gets highlighted and scrolled to while this clip plays. Text is curated from the on-page prose with light cleanup so it reads naturally aloud; the journey scrollytelling captions are intentionally omitted.

sections.text: Continuity — a colossal, four-and-a-half-metre-high granite sculpture shaped as an infinity loop, located in central Frankfurt, Germany. It was created by the Swiss architect and polymath Max Bill, who lived from 1908 to 1994, a prominent figure in modernism and concrete art.

Imagine a two-hundred-ton block of granite, extracted from a quarry in Sardinia in the 1980s, carved into a work of art and shipped across the North Atlantic, then transported through Europe via canals and rivers — before finally being installed as a monumental infinity loop in the heart of Frankfurt's financial district. Such an undertaking, combining production and logistics, had not been seen since the transport of colossal sculptures carved from monoliths in ancient Egypt. So what was the idea behind it, and what made it possible forty years ago?

In Continuity, I attempted to realize an idea that had long been present in my mind: the representation of an infinite space in infinite motion. Subsequently, I engaged with the problems realized in it, which are extraordinarily fascinating. That sculpture consists of a band of uniform width throughout, whose edges are therefore parallel. It thus appears to be a two-sided surface, separated from the surrounding space by parallel lines and forming a new space. The phenomenon of this body, however, is that this new space-forming surface has only a single side, and that the seemingly parallel two lines are in fact only one single line — that is, a line running parallel to itself.

In Continuity, I intended to achieve something similar: a surface, a boundary. Purely theoretically, from a twin band — one that is twisted one and a half times around itself and fused with another that is twisted only half a turn — one could obtain a form similar to the endless loop, but with only one surface and one boundary. For reasons unknown to me, this did not come about. Thus Continuity, despite a theoretically different expected result, consists of two parallel, bounded surfaces, composed of infinitely many straight lines.

This explanation may seem somewhat dry and primitive, yet it is the only thing I can say about it myself. I can, however, add that for me such a sculpture represents something like a knot in space, a point of concentration of various latent directions, and that through its existence space is ordered, newly formed, and given aim and direction.

There is continuity in our purpose. However, our purpose is also to see — and to see clearly. We designers are not working for the sake of machines, for some impersonal, superordinate entity such as industry, or state, or community. We are working for the wellbeing of every person, every individual, as part of a community. This purpose, this new humanism, is what I'd like to see as continuity. — Max Bill, Continuity and Change, 1953.
Max Bill, who lived from 1908 to 1994, was a great Swiss polymath: architect, industrial and graphic designer, sculptor, painter — and also a prolific writer, scholar, and teacher.

He attended the Bauhaus, where he was taught by Josef Albers, László Moholy-Nagy, Paul Klee, Wassily Kandinsky and Oskar Schlemmer. Bill remained closely associated with the Bauhaus school and was a key figure in developing and propagating its principles — as a guest lecturer at the Kunstgewerbeschule Zürich, and as a co-founder and first rector of the Ulm School of Design.
Why would one of Germany's leading banks decide to place a large sculpture in front of its headquarters?

As the Deutsche Bank Twin Towers rose in Frankfurt between 1979 and 1984, the bank's senior management faced a crucial question: what monumental artwork should stand at the threshold of the new headquarters? In 1981, while construction continued, the board began to search for a proper sculptor. Deutsche Bank had long committed to art and culture — a programme whose scope is evident today across the Towers' sixty floors, where the collection spans a hundred international artworks from more than forty countries.

The choice had to meet several criteria. The artist should come from the German-speaking countries. The work should fit Deutsche Bank's collecting profile, meaning significant contemporary art. It should relate less to the building's facade than to the plaza in front of it. And the artist should be free in his solution, while that solution still reflected the functions of the bank.

Few names fit better than Max Bill. An established Swiss artist and sculptor, modern and unexpected, his work corresponded closely to the bank's vision. Since his Bauhaus years, Bill had built an art of precise geometry, calculation and mathematics, carried through painting, sculpture and graphic work — an approach as innovative as it was rigorous.

Bill first proposed a coloured column, conceived to present the viewer with numbers and quantities. Yet when the board asked how he himself would decide in their place, he gave his preference to Continuity, the work recommended by the bank's art advisers.

The chance to finally bring this long-running hit, now approaching its fortieth anniversary, to life was so tempting that I cast aside all my reservations about its age, and a wave of almost insurmountable difficulties that was welling up inside me, and decided to take the plunge on this adventure. — Max Bill.

Kontinuität worked through contrast to the straight Twin Towers, while proposing harmony. The sculpture had once been destroyed by vandals in Zurich, and the idea of the unbroken continuity of world trade and banking — together with the restoration of art as a restoration of life in post-war Germany — suited the commission perfectly. The work was given to Max Bill.

Carving the large granite sculpture took three years. It required a second sculptor, Dominique Stroobant, charged with its realisation alongside the bank's management. Stroobant approached the task with rigour. He set up the firm, hired assistants, found a suitable quarry for the granite in Sardinia, and built a workshop in the port of Carrara, working for three years always in consultation with, and under the supervision of, Max Bill.

At haus bill — the home where Max Bill's widow Angela Thomas lives today — we found a large archive of documentation, accounts and invoices connected to the sculpture. Stroobant was responsible for the entire management: the extensive correspondence with Deutsche Bank over shipments, the selection and ordering of transport, the payment of invoices, the preparations for the opening, and the accompanying exhibition.

It is precisely these documents — the notebooks, drawings, draft letters, expense calculations and photographs of the work in progress — that allow us today to understand the full complexity of realising such an ambitious idea. Stroobant did not simply make the sculpture: he coordinated an entire logistics operation, smoothed away bureaucratic obstacles, and ensured quality at every stage. Deutsche Bank, for its part, placed its trust in his experience and his sense of responsibility.

At the sculpture's inauguration in 1986, Herbert Zapp — board member and initiator of the Deutsche Bank art collection programme, who had begun acquiring works to fill the bank's buildings seven years earlier — said:

Max Bill's sculpture does not simply correspond to the bank building — it occupies an urbanistically significant setting, and will be seen and rediscovered daily by many people. Whether from a car, a park bench, on foot, from the Opernplatz or from the Taunusanlage: from every angle, and for everyone who takes pleasure in it, this granite sculpture with its infinite loop is meant to be an offering, a point of reference. — Herbert Zapp.

Deutsche Bank's investment in art was never purely aesthetic. It reflected a broader conviction — that cultural engagement is part of what an institution owes to its people and to society, building cultural capital that extends from the workplace to the city and beyond. Kontinuität is perhaps the most eloquent expression of that idea: a sculpture whose name speaks to the unbroken continuity of this commitment.

In 1981, Max Bill met the young and energetic sculptor and photographer Dominique Stroobant. This encounter grew into a lifelong friendship. Their greatest challenge would become the project Continuity — the development of which took three years.

Stroobant was responsible for the entire production process: from planning the transportation route of a massive block of granite, to the creation of the full-scale, four-metre sculpture together with his team of four sculptors.

Dominique Stroobant is a Belgian artist and mathematician known for his work at the intersection of geometry, perception and conceptual art. His practice explores spatial structures, continuity, and transformation — often translating abstract mathematical principles into precise visual or sculptural expressions.

Max Bill was consistently inspired by mathematics and logic in art. His approach, which he called verifiable logic, guided him from early experimentation toward a precise method of making — and explaining — his work: You can always understand my work, even if you don't like it. From the beginning of his career, Bill was fascinated by the Möbius strip. From his first attempts in 1936 to the realization of Continuity in Frankfurt, he produced dozens — if not hundreds — of variations on the infinity loop, exploring differences in scale, material, and environment.

But how are we to understand the topology of Continuity? Is it a Möbius strip, a variation on an endless loop, or simply an artistic, sculptural interpretation of an infinite motif? In short, how did he do it? Even though Bill left some explanations, our own experiments and consultations with mathematicians did not yield an immediate understanding of how the sculpture was conceived and modeled.

In Continuity, I intended to achieve something similar — a single surface, a single boundary. Theoretically, a double helix, twisted twice by half a turn and fused with one twisted only half a turn, should have resulted in something akin to an infinite loop, possessing only one surface and one boundary. For reasons unknown to me, this did not happen, so Continuity, despite the theoretically expected outcome, consists of two parallel bounded surfaces composed of infinitely many straight lines. This explanation may sound somewhat dry and simplistic, yet it is the only thing I can say about it myself. — Max Bill.

The interesting thing to note is that Bill thought he had invented a completely new shape. Even more curious was that he discovered it by twisting a strip of paper, just as Möbius had done many years previously. Not long afterwards, people began to congratulate me on my fresh and original interpretation of the Egyptian symbol for infinity and the Möbius ribbon. I had never heard of either of them. My mathematical knowledge had never gone beyond routine architectural calculations, and I had no great interest in mathematics.

The mathematician Barry Cipra observed: Bill's intuition that a single half twist connected to a double half twist should result in a single-sided, single-edge surface is quite correct; depending on the handedness of the twists, the loop you wind up with has either three twists or one. So it's a mystery how he managed to add one and two and get four.

By carefully examining the sculpture itself and creating a 3D model using 360-degree video and photography, and by comparing it with Bill's metal sculpture from 1945 to 46 — used by him as a one-to-twenty prototype — we were able to analyze the work and conduct a series of spatial experiments. One of these resulted in an origami model that follows the original topology step by step and, surprisingly, resolves into a clear infinity-loop construction. The result is striking: a pure mathematical model transforms into a work of art.
